values.goal: Understand 3D Gaussian data and the projection and compositing paths, and design a fault-tolerant viewer using small data with verified provenance.
values.capstone: A local GS viewer with a fixed camera path, loading states, a selection policy, and a quality comparison report

values.title: 3DGS Representations and Data
values.prerequisites: Three.js cameras and projection, and alpha blending
values.environment: The existing gaussian-splatting-01 preview is a starting point. It does not replace implementation or verification of the full subsequent assignment. This is a document-guided exercise in a separate local project. Use only small data you create or local files whose usage permission you have checked. The existing preview is a CPU teaching viewer for .splat/ASCII GS PLY files of at most 1 MiB and 512 items; it is not a Spark GPU renderer.
values.concepts.0.title: Representation primitives
values.concepts.0.explanation: A mesh stores surface connectivity, while a Gaussian stores a distribution in space. Their storage and rendering paths also differ from NeRF neural network queries.
values.concepts.1.title: Parameters
values.concepts.1.explanation: Position alone cannot reconstruct a Gaussian's shape and color. Examine the meaning of scale, rotation, opacity, and the color representation together.
values.outcomes.0: Explain the differences between the three scene representations.
values.outcomes.1: Classify the roles of Gaussian attributes.
values.steps.0: In representation.md, tabulate the inputs and rendered outputs of mesh, NeRF, and 3DGS.
values.steps.1: In data.js, define two Gaussians with position, scale, quaternion, opacity, and color.
values.steps.2: Trace how scale and opacity in the existing gaussian-splatting-01 CPU example produce the 2D radial gradient output. Examine the 3D projection implementation separately in the gaussian-splatting-02 viewer.
values.variables.0.name: scale
values.variables.0.expected: Expect only the width along the ellipse's axis to increase, with the center unchanged.
values.criteria.0: Write at least one line each describing the storage primitives and rendering paths of the three representations.
values.criteria.1: List all required attributes and units for the two Gaussians.
values.questions.0: Which attributes are missing from an ordinary point cloud?
values.questions.1: Which inputs must be recalculated when the camera moves?
values.references.0.title: Spark Official Documentation
values.references.1.title: 3D Gaussian Splatting Research Project

values.concepts.1.title: Scope limits

values.concepts.0.explanation: If the camera and data use different up axes, the scene appears tilted. Specify the axis conversion as a data transformation matrix rather than hiding it through camera manipulation.
values.concepts.1.title: Scale reference
values.concepts.1.explanation: The length units of a reconstruction may not correspond to actual meters. Use a reference object or explicitly defined virtual units.

values.concepts.0.title: Representing rotation
values.concepts.0.explanation: A quaternion must maintain unit length to represent a rotation. The component order in a file may differ from the library constructor's order.
values.concepts.1.title: Anisotropy
values.concepts.1.explanation: If the three scale values differ, width varies with direction. For an isotropic Gaussian, changing the rotation leaves the shape unchanged.

values.concepts.0.title: Covariance
values.concepts.0.explanation: Combining rotation with per-axis variances represents an ellipsoid in space. When scale is interpreted as standard deviation, variance uses its square.
values.concepts.1.title: Symmetry
values.concepts.1.explanation: Covariance must be symmetric, and valid variances cannot be negative. Projecting invalid inputs directly makes numerical calculations unstable.
values.steps.0: In covariance.js, calculate R·diag(scale²)·Rᵀ.
values.steps.1: Save the 3×3 results for axis-aligned scale and rotated scale as JSON.
values.steps.2: Print the symmetry error and the rejection result for negative scale inputs.

values.criteria.0: The maximum difference between symmetric elements is at most 1e-6.
values.criteria.1: Numerically confirm that doubling scale quadruples variance.
values.questions.0: What changes if scale is confused with variance?
values.questions.1: If covariance is stored, is separate rotation information needed?

values.concepts.0.title: Perspective projection
values.concepts.0.explanation: A nearby Gaussian appears larger even at the same world-space size. Screen covariance must reflect the local rate of change of the projection.
values.concepts.1.title: Near plane
values.concepts.1.explanation: Points behind the camera or near the near plane cannot be handled safely through simple division. Check visibility limits and finite values before projection.
values.outcomes.0: Distinguish world-space size from screen-space size.
values.steps.0: In project.js, separate the view-space transformation from the perspective divide.
values.steps.1: Project identical Gaussians at depths 2 and 4 and print their screen centers and radii.
values.steps.2: Supply inputs on either side of the near plane and behind the camera, and record whether they are excluded.

values.variables.0.expected: Expect the screen width of a small Gaussian to be approximately halved.
values.criteria.0: Calculate the screen-width ratio at the two depths.
values.criteria.1: No NaN or Infinity remains in screen coordinates for the three boundary inputs.
values.questions.0: Is the linear approximation accurate for large Gaussians too?
values.questions.1: If the center is off screen, is the entire Gaussian invisible?

values.concepts.0.title: Kernel
values.concepts.0.explanation: A Gaussian's weight decreases with distance from its center. Use covariance-normalized distance rather than pixel distance to preserve the ellipse.
values.concepts.1.title: Opacity
values.concepts.1.explanation: Opacity combines with the kernel weight to produce pixel alpha. Even when the apparent total is similar, changing size and changing opacity have different effects.

values.variables.0.expected: Expect center alpha to double while the ellipse's normalized distance structure stays unchanged.
values.criteria.0: The center weight is 1, and the four values decrease as distance increases.
values.criteria.1: Record the center-alpha ratio before and after changing opacity.
values.questions.0: What artifacts appear if the kernel is cut off at a finite radius?
values.questions.1: Why is causal analysis harder when scale and opacity change together?

values.concepts.0.title: Compositing
values.concepts.0.explanation: Translucent splats of different colors produce different colors depending on draw order. Simply adding colors cannot reproduce occlusion.
values.concepts.1.title: Consistent representations
values.concepts.1.explanation: Whether alpha is premultiplied determines both color storage and the compositing equation. Mixing conventions makes boundaries too dark or too bright.

values.concepts.0.title: Center sorting
values.concepts.0.explanation: Sorting by center depth is simple, but it does not guarantee the correct per-pixel order for large, overlapping ellipsoids. Observe the moments when order changes as the camera rotates.
values.concepts.1.title: Stability
values.concepts.1.explanation: A stable secondary key for items at the same depth can reduce unnecessary order jitter. It does not solve geometric sorting errors.
values.outcomes.1: Observe the limits of the sorting approximation.

values.concepts.0.title: View dependence
values.concepts.0.explanation: SH coefficients represent color that varies with direction. Using only the constant term removes view-dependent changes.
values.concepts.1.title: Degree and evidence
values.concepts.1.explanation: Increasing the degree does not improve quality if the source lacks valid coefficients. Compare memory, computation, and actually observed quality together.
values.outcomes.0: Explain the view dependence of SH.
values.outcomes.1: Distinguish degree from claims about quality.

values.criteria.0: Save RGB for the six directions.
values.criteria.1: In constant-term mode, color differences across directions are at most 1e-6.

values.title: Sorting Update Intervals
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and records from Unit 16. Before the Sorting Update Intervals experiment, preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs.
values.environment: First check the execution scope guidance on the example screen. The following describes the environment needed to extend the assignment in a separate project. This is a document-guided exercise in a separate local project. Use only small data you create or local files whose usage permission you have checked. The existing preview is a CPU teaching viewer for .splat/ASCII GS PLY files of at most 1 MiB and 512 items; it is not a Spark GPU renderer.
values.concepts.0.title: Reuse
values.concepts.0.explanation: Depth order can be reused when the camera is stationary. Using stale order while the camera moves can increase compositing errors.
values.concepts.1.title: Observing delay
values.concepts.1.explanation: Sorting less frequently reduces CPU work but can delay the visual response. Average time alone does not reveal these changes.
values.steps.0: In scheduler.js, create sorting modes for every frame and every 4 frames.
values.steps.1: Play the same camera-path.json in both modes.
values.steps.2: Record sort counts, CPU time, and image differences at order-update moments.
values.variables.0.name: Sorting interval
values.variables.0.expected: Expect fewer sorting calls and more traces of stale order during fast rotation.
values.criteria.0: Compare sorting call counts over playback of the same duration.
values.criteria.1: Keep images from two intervals where order changes.
values.questions.0: What does an update policy based on camera movement improve?
values.questions.1: Can reduced sorting time be treated directly as an improvement to the whole frame?

values.title: Resolution and Pixel Workload
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and records from Unit 17. Before the Resolution and Pixel Workload experiment, preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs.

values.concepts.0.title: Pixel cost
values.concepts.0.explanation: Reducing screen resolution lowers the number of pixels evaluated even with the same Gaussian count. It also changes silhouettes and thin structures.
values.concepts.1.title: Comparison conditions
values.concepts.1.explanation: Record CSS dimensions separately from actual drawing buffer dimensions. Mixing cameras or DPR values makes it hard to judge the effect of resolution.
values.outcomes.1: Compare quality loss at identical viewpoints.
values.steps.0: In quality.js, add fixed CSS dimensions and a render scale input.
values.steps.1: Fix camera-path.json and the data id, and play at scales 1.0 and 0.5.
values.steps.2: Save actual buffer dimensions, median frame interval, and images of thin structures.
values.variables.0.name: render scale
values.variables.0.expected: Expect approximately 1/4 as many pixels but less detail.
values.criteria.0: Record width×height for both modes.
values.criteria.1: Annotate detail loss in three images from identical times.
values.questions.0: Why is frame time not directly proportional to pixel count?
values.questions.1: How do DPR and render scale combine?

values.title: Reducing Gaussian Count
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and records from Unit 18. Before the Reducing Gaussian Count experiment, preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs.
values.environment: First check the execution scope guidance on the example screen. The following describes the environment needed to extend the assignment in a separate project. values.concepts.0.title: Subset selection
values.concepts.0.explanation: Reducing item count lowers storage and sorting work. Random removal may disproportionately damage thin structures or low-opacity regions.
values.concepts.1.title: Reproducibility
values.concepts.1.explanation: Using different random values each time makes reduction strategies hard to compare. Save the seed and selected ids to use the same subset.
values.outcomes.1: Evaluate the visual impact of reduction strategies.
values.steps.0: In subset.js, implement seeded selection and selection ordered by opacity.
values.steps.1: From a synthetic fixture of 256 items, select 128 and save the id list.
values.steps.2: Compare empty regions, sorting time, and file bytes at the same three viewpoints.
values.variables.0.name: Retained count
values.variables.0.expected: Expect less sorting work but more holes in some regions.
values.criteria.0: Using the same seed twice produces identical id lists.
values.criteria.1: Compare images at three viewpoints for both selection strategies.
values.questions.0: Are low-opacity items always less important?
values.questions.1: How does pruning during training differ from simply reducing a file?

values.concepts.0.title: Color calculations
values.concepts.0.explanation: Compositing in linear space and converting colors for display are different operations. Applying color conversion twice distorts brightness comparisons.
values.concepts.1.title: Background dependence
values.concepts.1.explanation: Transparent regions look different depending on background color. Fix the background and alpha display policy for quality comparisons too.
values.outcomes.0: Distinguish compositing space from display space.
values.steps.0: In color.js, add comments specifying the compositing space and the location of the final display conversion.
values.steps.1: Composite a gray translucent fixture over black and white backgrounds.
values.steps.2: Save a table of input RGB, composited RGB, and display RGB at each stage.
values.variables.0.name: Background
values.variables.0.expected: Expect the brightness of transmitted regions to differ even for the same splat.
values.criteria.0: Record values at the three color stages and the number of conversions.
values.criteria.1: Confirm that the same opacity is used on both backgrounds.
values.questions.0: Which test values can reveal duplicate color conversion?
values.questions.1: Can two screenshots with different backgrounds be used to compare quality?

values.title: Defining Quality Evaluation Criteria
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and records from Unit 20. Before the Defining Quality Evaluation Criteria experiment, preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs.
values.environment: First check the execution scope guidance on the example screen. The following describes the environment needed to extend the assignment in a separate project. The existing preview is a CPU teaching viewer for .splat/ASCII GS PLY files of at most 1 MiB and 512 items; it is not a Spark GPU renderer.
values.concepts.0.title: Reference image
values.concepts.0.explanation: Interpretation depends on whether the reference is synthetic or an actual observed photograph. Do not call image differences calculated without ground-truth photographs reconstruction accuracy.
values.concepts.1.title: Multiple observations
values.concepts.1.explanation: A single average error can hide thin structures or flicker. Evaluate specified regions together with a camera path.
values.outcomes.1: Interpret numerical and visual evidence together.
values.steps.0: In evaluation.json, define three viewpoints, two regions of interest, and a background.
values.steps.1: Save identically sized ImageData for baseline and reduction modes.
values.steps.2: In report.md, write the mean absolute channel difference and describe losses in the regions of interest.
values.variables.0.name: Evaluation region
values.variables.0.expected: Expect local losses to stand out more than in the overall average.
values.criteria.0: Use the same ROI coordinates at the three viewpoints.
values.criteria.1: Write at least two items each for numerical differences and visual descriptions.
values.questions.0: What does a difference metric mean if the reference image is wrong?
values.questions.1: Which errors does still-image evaluation miss?

values.title: Separating Profiling Intervals
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and records from Unit 21. Before the Separating Profiling Intervals experiment, preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs.
values.environment: First check the execution scope guidance on the example screen. The following describes the environment needed to extend the assignment in a separate project. values.concepts.0.title: Stage costs
values.concepts.0.explanation: Reading, parsing, sorting, projection, and compositing can have different bottlenecks. Total loading time alone makes it hard to identify what needs improvement.
values.concepts.1.title: Measurement range
values.concepts.1.explanation: performance.now measures elapsed time for CPU intervals. When using a GPU renderer, do not call this value GPU execution time.
values.outcomes.1: Distinguish CPU and GPU timing claims.
values.steps.0: In metrics.js, add start and end markers for each stage.
values.steps.1: After warm-up, process the same fixture five times and create a table by stage.
values.steps.2: Keep CPU teaching viewer results and separate Spark experiment results in different files.
values.variables.0.name: Data count
values.variables.0.expected: Expect sorting and projection intervals to increase, while compositing is also affected by screen area.
values.criteria.0: Save stage times and environment information for the five runs.
values.criteria.1: Label unmeasured GPU execution time as unmeasured.
values.questions.0: Why can total time differ from the sum of stage times?
values.questions.1: Can a CPU viewer bottleneck be applied directly to Spark?

values.concepts.0.title: Ownership
values.concepts.0.explanation: Removing scene objects and releasing their associated resources are separate operations. Keep a list of who created each buffer, texture, and listener.
values.concepts.1.title: Repeated use
values.concepts.1.explanation: A viewer that works once may reveal leaks after repeated replacement and shutdown. Check renderer-specific cleanup APIs in the documentation for that version.
values.steps.0: In lifecycle.js, register created resources and their cleanup functions.
values.steps.1: Replace small fixtures A/B ten times, then call dispose twice.
values.steps.2: Record active listener, animation loop, and object counts, and clear references.
values.variables.0.name: Replacement count
values.variables.0.expected: Expect active loops and current data references not to accumulate when cleanup is correct.
values.criteria.0: There is at most one active render loop after replacement.
values.criteria.1: Repeated dispose completes without exceptions and leaves a cleanup list.
values.questions.0: Why is scene.remove alone insufficient?
values.questions.1: How do library caches differ from actual leaks?
